newsitem.title: USA: Washington wedding to link Fed chief, reporter.
newsitem.headline: Washington wedding to link Fed chief, reporter.

text.p: Federal Reserve Board chairman Alan Greenspan can speak so ambiguously that the first two or three times he proposed marriage, his bride-to-be says now, "I just didn't get it."

Finally last Christmas Day, the Delphic central banker, 71, made his intentions clear, and the man often said to be the second-most powerful person in America will wed NBC-TV reporter Andrea Mitchell, 50, on April 6.
The merger is considered the wedding-of-the-year in the nation's capital. It will be held in the Washington area, but Mitchell would not say exactly where.

And despite Greenspan's recent attempts at plainer speaking, no one expects him to reveal the wedding site either. With less than two weeks to go until the vows are exchanged, he has been busy raising interest rates.

The Federal Reserve lifted a key rate Tuesday for the first time in over two years in an effort to stay a step ahead of inflation. The rate increase is likely to lead to higher borrowing costs for many people.
But Mitchell quipped: "I don't have to worry about interest rates." She and Greenspan won't be taking out a mortgage since they plan to live at the Washington home she already owns.

The couple has been dating for 12 years and are a fixture on the Washington social scene -- a familiar sight at top-drawer embassy parties or events like the annual dinner of the Gridiron Club, a prestigious journalists' society.

But their friends say they are nonetheless thrilled to be tying the knot. Mitchell, who covers foreign affairs and intelligence matters for NBC and is known as a tough and aggressive reporter, is "walking on air," said Helen Thomas, UPI's veteran White House correspondent.

"She's very happy, and he looks very happy. It's nice to see love in bloom," said Thomas, who attended a congratulatory luncheon for Mitchell this month where play money embossed with photos of Greenspan was strewn across the tables.

This is the second marriage for both. Neither has children, although Mitchell has a godchild, the daughter of two other journalists -- Al Hunt of the Wall Street Journal and Judy Woodruff of Cable News Network.

The marriage will be a private civil ceremony and Mitchell says her dress will be "simple and low-key." Greenspan, she said, plans to wear "a plain suit. I've lost the battle for him to get a new suit."
Her main worry is "just about having it private, and not having it rain. I wouldn't want it rainy."
Why, then, did they select a day in April for the wedding? "Both of us were in town," said Mitchell, who, like her husband-to-be, has a job that requires a lot of travel.

"We realised that one of the requirements is that you can't get married if both are travelling. You both have to be in the same place," said Mitchell. She spoke to Reuters by phone while en route to the airport for another business trip.

So what is the inscrutable Greenspan really like? Economists, public officials and financial markets here and abroad pore over his words, trying to divine their meaning to determine the future direction of U.S. monetary policy. At times Greenspan seems to want to keep everyone guessing.

"I spend the substantial amount of my time endeavouring to fend off questions ... worrying that I might be too clear," he said in 1995. "What I've learned ... is a new language called 'Fed-speak.' We learn to mumble with great incoherence."
So Mitchell said Greenspan claims that when he first tried to broach the subject of marriage, she didn't get his meaning. "He's a man who's very careful with his words," she said.
But there's a kind person beneath the Fed-speak, his fiancee said.
"He's very shy. He's a man of tremendous character, and he's very, very kind. And very funny -- many people may not realise that," she said.
They will not take a honeymoon right away. "We're going to delay that a couple of months until we can both get away," she said. Will it be Europe or Japan? The markets are watching.
